setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall with fingertips lightly touching for balance. Feet hip-width apart, slight knee softness permitted.
execution_cues: Rise onto toes and hold at approximately 70% effort
Maintain even pressure through both feet
Breathe normally throughout hold
Keep knees soft — do not lock out
contraindications_or_cautions: Reduce hold duration or range if pain exceeds 3/10. Not suitable if rest pain >7/10.
patient_facing_explanation: This hold loads your Achilles tendon without movement. Research shows it reliably reduces pain for 45+ minutes. It is safe to use even when your tendon is most irritable.
clinician_notes: First-line exercise for high irritability. Produces cortical analgesia via descending pain inhibition. 70% MVIC target. Can be used pre-activity for pain priming. Bilateral before unilateral.

setup_instructions: Stand on one leg with fingertips lightly touching a wall. Rise onto toes of the affected leg and hold.
execution_cues: Hold at 70% effort — strong but controlled
Keep standing knee slightly soft
Do not grip the floor with toes
Maintain upright posture throughout hold
common_compensations: Hip hiking to compensate for calf fatigue
contraindications_or_cautions: Do not progress to unilateral if bilateral isometric is not yet pain-controlled. Reduce to bilateral if pain exceeds 4/10.
patient_facing_explanation: The single-leg version of the isometric hold increases the load through your Achilles tendon specifically. It keeps all the pain-relieving benefits while preparing you for single-leg activities.
clinician_notes: Progress from ex_001 when bilateral isometric is consistently ≤2/10. Unilateral increases tendon load substantially. Monitor pain response closely on first session.

setup_instructions: Stand with knees bent to approximately 30-40 degrees, holding wall or chair for support. Rise onto toes in this bent-knee position and hold.
execution_cues: Keep knees bent throughout the hold
Rise as high as possible in the bent-knee position
Hold at 70% effort
Maintain equal weight distribution
contraindications_or_cautions: Preferred over straight-knee variant for isolated soleus loading. Safe for insertional presentations at all irritability levels.
patient_facing_explanation: The bent-knee version targets the deeper calf muscle (soleus) more specifically, which attaches closer to your heel. It is safe even when your tendon is most sensitive.
clinician_notes: Soleus-dominant isometric. Critical for insertional presentations where straight-knee loading at range provokes compression. Use alongside ex_001 as paired isometric protocol.

setup_instructions: Sit in a chair with feet flat on floor. Push ball of foot into floor (or against resistance band) and hold.
execution_cues: Press firmly into floor without moving foot
Aim for 70% maximum effort
Keep heel on floor
Breathe normally
common_compensations: Pushing with toes rather than ball of foot
contraindications_or_cautions: Lowest-demand entry point. Use when standing isometrics are not tolerated.
patient_facing_explanation: The seated version is the gentlest way to load your Achilles. It is the starting point when standing exercises are too painful, or as a first step after a flare.
clinician_notes: Minimum viable isometric. For very high irritability (rest pain 5-7/10) or post-flare. Load is modest but provides mechanical stimulus and pain education. Progress to standing isometrics as soon as tolerated.

exercise_name: Supported Standing Calf Raise — Partial Range
setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall with both hands on wall for support. Rise onto toes through a comfortable, pain-free range only.
execution_cues: Move only within your pain-free range
Rise slowly over 2 seconds, lower slowly over 2 seconds
Use wall firmly for support
Stop range of motion before pain starts
common_compensations: Pushing through pain to reach full range
Using arms to offload body weight excessively
contraindications_or_cautions: Range should be restricted to pain-free only. Do not attempt full range if painful.
patient_facing_explanation: A gentle calf raise through a comfortable range. This bridges from holds to full movement. Go only as far as feels comfortable — the range will increase as your tendon settles.
clinician_notes: Transition exercise between isometric loading and full-range isotonic. Range-of-motion gate is patient-guided. Progress range before progressing load.

exercise_name: Leg Press Calf Raise — Short-Range Isometric
setup_instructions: Set up on leg press with feet on platform at shoulder width. Extend through toes to plantarflexion mid-range and hold. Apply moderate resistance via machine.
execution_cues: Hold at mid-range plantarflexion — not end range
Apply approximately 70% maximum effort
Do not allow platform to move
Breathe normally
common_compensations: Holding at end-range rather than mid-range
contraindications_or_cautions: Set resistance at a comfortable working load. Avoid end-range compression in insertional presentations.
patient_facing_explanation: Using the leg press machine allows us to control exactly how much load goes through your Achilles during the hold. This is a gym-based alternative with greater load control.
clinician_notes: High load potential makes this useful for patients who need more stimulus than bodyweight isometrics provide but cannot tolerate dynamic loading. Load can be precisely titrated.

setup_instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Rise up onto toes through full range, lower under control. Can be performed on flat ground or edge of step.
execution_cues: Rise up tall through full range
Lower slowly — 2-3 seconds on the way down
Pause briefly at top
Maintain even weight through both feet
contraindications_or_cautions: Not suitable for insertional Achilles presentations in early phase — dorsiflexion at base of range compresses the insertion. Use flat-ground version to limit dorsiflexion if borderline.
patient_facing_explanation: The standard bilateral calf raise builds strength and resilience in both your Achilles tendon and calf muscles. This is one of the most important exercises in your programme.
clinician_notes: Entry-level isotonic. Insertional precaution: limit range to neutral if presenting with insertional AT. Progress tempo (2-1-2 → 3-1-3) before adding load.

setup_instructions: Stand on one leg with toes on edge of step or flat ground. Rise onto toes through full range and lower under control.
execution_cues: Rise tall — reach maximum plantarflexion
Control the lowering phase over 3 seconds
Avoid trunk rotation or lateral lean
Fingertips on wall for balance only
common_compensations: Bending knee to cheat range of motion
contraindications_or_cautions: Insertional precaution — limit to flat-ground version if insertional presentation. Progress from bilateral only.
patient_facing_explanation: The single-leg calf raise is the key strength benchmark for your Achilles. It builds the capacity needed for walking, running, and sport. Working on this consistently is central to your recovery.
clinician_notes: Key functional strength benchmark — 25 single-leg raises to full range is a running readiness indicator. Progress tempo before adding external load.

setup_instructions: Stand with knees bent 30-40 degrees. Rise onto toes through available range while maintaining knee bend.
execution_cues: Keep knees bent throughout
Rise as high as possible in the bent-knee position
Lower slowly
Equal weight through both feet
common_compensations: Straightening knees on the way up
Reduced range due to early knee extension
contraindications_or_cautions: Preferred over straight-knee variant for soleus isolation. Safe for insertional presentations.
patient_facing_explanation: The bent-knee raise isolates the deeper calf muscle that runs directly into your Achilles tendon near the heel. It is gentler on the insertion and an important part of complete tendon loading.
clinician_notes: Soleus-biased isotonic. Pairs with ex_007 for comprehensive gastrocnemius + soleus loading. Insertional-safe due to reduced dorsiflexion at base position.

required_equipment: seated calf raise machine or weighted barbell on knees
setup_instructions: Sit on a bench or calf raise machine with weight on thighs just above knees. Rise onto toes and lower under control.
execution_cues: Full plantarflexion range
Slow lowering phase
Do not let heel slam down
Keep weight evenly distributed
contraindications_or_cautions: Knee flexion position means minimal gastrocnemius contribution — primarily soleus loading. Insertional safe.
patient_facing_explanation: The seated calf raise in the gym specifically targets the soleus — the muscle that works hardest during walking and running. Adding load here is important for building real tendon capacity.
clinician_notes: High load potential for soleus via seated position. Gastrocnemius contribution minimal at 90° knee flexion. Can be loaded heavily as tendon tolerance improves. Insertional-safe throughout.

setup_instructions: Sit on leg press with feet positioned at shoulder-width on lower portion of platform. Extend through toes in full plantarflexion range.
execution_cues: Push through toes to full plantarflexion
Return slowly to neutral — do not go past neutral into dorsiflexion
Control the pace — do not bounce
Maintain foot contact with platform throughout
common_compensations: Going into full dorsiflexion at base — avoid in insertional presentations
Allowing knees to flex during the movement
contraindications_or_cautions: Limit range of motion to neutral at base position for insertional presentations — avoid forced dorsiflexion.
patient_facing_explanation: The leg press calf raise lets us load your Achilles with significantly more weight in a safe, controlled position. It builds the tendon strength needed for heavier activities.
clinician_notes: Useful early isotonic for patients where standing balance or pain limits floor-based raises. Range gate important for insertional: set limiter to prevent full dorsiflexion.

exercise_name: Tempo Calf Raise with Pause at Top
setup_instructions: Standard bilateral calf raise position. Rise to peak plantarflexion over 3 seconds, hold at top for 2 seconds, lower slowly over 3 seconds.
execution_cues: Count to 3 on the way up
Hold hard at top — squeeze calf
Count to 3 on the way down
Do not rest at the bottom — maintain tension
contraindications_or_cautions: Full dorsiflexion at base — insertional precaution applies.
patient_facing_explanation: The pause at the top forces your calf and Achilles to work harder for longer. This builds both strength and tendon resilience more effectively than standard calf raises.
clinician_notes: High time-under-tension variant. Isometric component at top drives additional tendon adaptation. Good bridge between standard isotonic and loaded HSR.

exercise_name: Tempo Calf Raise with Slow Lowering
setup_instructions: Rise up onto toes using both legs over 2 seconds. Lower slowly using both legs (or single leg if tolerated) over 6 seconds.
execution_cues: Control every millimetre of the lowering phase
6 full seconds from top to bottom
Maintain tension throughout — do not drop
Feel the calf working during the lowering
common_compensations: Leaning forward to reduce calf load
contraindications_or_cautions: Eccentric component drives greater tendon stimulus. Insertional precaution at base of range.
patient_facing_explanation: Slowing down the lowering phase is one of the most powerful ways to strengthen your Achilles tendon. The eccentric phase drives the most tendon adaptation.
clinician_notes: Eccentric-biased isotonic. Good bridge to formal Alfredson protocol. Bilateral lowering reduces load compared to single-leg off-step — use as stepping stone.

setup_instructions: Position under Smith machine bar with toes on raised platform. Perform full range calf raise with bar resting across upper trapezius/shoulders.
execution_cues: Full range — up and down
3-1-3 tempo throughout
Progressively load to RPE 8 on final rep
Maintain vertical shin path
contraindications_or_cautions: Gym-dependent. Insertional precaution. Requires low irritability and established tolerance to bilateral raises.
patient_facing_explanation: Using the Smith machine allows us to safely add significant load to your calf raise. This level of loading is what drives the strongest Achilles tendon adaptations.
clinician_notes: High load potential. Smith machine path stabilises movement for heavy loading. Progress to 4x6-8 at RPE 8 for maximum tendon adaptation. Pairs with ex_020 (seated) for comprehensive loading.

setup_instructions: Stand with both feet on edge of step, toes on edge, heels free. Rise onto both toes, shift weight to affected leg, lower heel below step level over 6 seconds.
execution_cues: Rise using both legs — lower using one
6 full seconds on every repetition
Lower heel as far below step as comfortable
Feel the stretch in the calf
contraindications_or_cautions: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles tendinopathy in early/mid phase — forced dorsiflexion compresses the insertion. For midportion only.
patient_facing_explanation: This is the classic Alfredson eccentric exercise — one of the most studied treatments for Achilles tendon problems. Lowering slowly below step height is what makes it effective.
clinician_notes: Alfredson eccentric protocol. Some pain during exercise is acceptable (≤5/10 by original protocol). CONTRAINDICATED for insertional AT. Twice-daily dosing supported by original RCT.

setup_instructions: Same position as ex_015 but maintain approximately 30° knee bend throughout. Rise using both legs with bent knee, lower on one leg maintaining knee bend.
execution_cues: Keep knee bent throughout the entire rep
Same 6-second lowering as straight-knee variant
Feel the load in the deeper calf muscle
Maintain consistent knee angle
common_compensations: Reduced range compared to straight-knee variant
contraindications_or_cautions: Soleus eccentric — same insertional contraindication applies due to dorsiflexion at base. Midportion only.
patient_facing_explanation: The bent-knee version targets the soleus specifically. Performing both the straight-knee and bent-knee version gives full coverage of your Achilles tendon from all angles.
clinician_notes: Soleus-targeting eccentric — should be performed alongside ex_015 for complete Alfredson protocol coverage. Same dosing and insertional contraindication.

exercise_name: Assisted Up — Single-Leg Down Calf Raise
setup_instructions: Flat ground version. Rise onto toes using both legs, transfer weight to affected leg, lower slowly on single leg. Return to start using both legs.
execution_cues: Use both legs equally on the way up
Shift weight smoothly before lowering
Lower over 4 seconds on single leg
Control every part of the descent
common_compensations: Using unaffected leg to assist on the way down
contraindications_or_cautions: Flat ground version significantly reduces dorsiflexion compared to step version — more insertional-friendly but still use caution.
patient_facing_explanation: This exercise gives you the benefits of single-leg lowering on flat ground, making it less demanding than the step version. It's a good stepping stone toward full eccentric loading.
clinician_notes: Eccentric with assisted concentric — reduces fatigue accumulation and allows higher rep completion. Flat ground reduces dorsiflexion range compared to step. Good bridge to ex_015.

setup_instructions: Set up on leg press. Use both feet to push to full plantarflexion, then lower slowly back to neutral (do not go into dorsiflexion for insertional presentations) over 5 seconds.
execution_cues: Both feet up — controlled lowering
5 seconds on the way down
Stop at neutral — do not force dorsiflexion
Maintain control throughout the range
common_compensations: Allowing dorsiflexion past neutral in insertional cases
contraindications_or_cautions: Insertional-safe if range is limited to neutral at base. Do not allow forced dorsiflexion.
patient_facing_explanation: The leg press eccentric is the safest way to get heavy eccentric loading if you have insertional tendon pain, because we can control exactly how far your ankle moves.
clinician_notes: Insertional-safe eccentric via ROM control. High load potential. Load can exceed bodyweight — useful when floor-based eccentrics cannot be adequately loaded.

setup_instructions: Hold dumbbell(s) or place barbell on shoulders. Perform full range calf raise on flat ground or raised surface with 3-1-3 tempo.
execution_cues: Load to RPE 8 on final rep of each set
3 seconds up — 1 second hold — 3 seconds down
Full range
No bounce at bottom
contraindications_or_cautions: Low irritability only. Insertional precaution. Requires established tolerance to slow bodyweight raises.
patient_facing_explanation: Adding external weight to your calf raise is what drives the most powerful changes in your Achilles tendon. Research shows this type of heavy, slow loading is one of the best treatments available.
clinician_notes: HSR protocol. Target RPE 8 on final rep. Load progression: +2.5-5kg weekly when full sets completed. Pairs with ex_020 for comprehensive gastrocnemius + soleus HSR.

required_equipment: seated calf raise machine or barbell/dumbbell on knees
setup_instructions: Heavy load on knees in seated position. Perform full plantarflexion range with 3-1-3 tempo.
execution_cues: Load to RPE 8 on final rep
Full range — complete plantarflexion
3 seconds down — maintain tension
No bounce
contraindications_or_cautions: Insertional-safe due to knee flexion position. Requires low irritability.
patient_facing_explanation: Heavy seated raises load the soleus to maximum capacity. Because you're seated, this is safe even with insertional tendon pain. It's a key exercise for building the deep calf strength that protects your Achilles.
clinician_notes: HSR soleus. Insertional-safe throughout loading range. Pairs with ex_019 (standing/gastroc) for Beyer HSR protocol. Progress load weekly.

exercise_name: Heavy Single-Leg Calf Raise with Dumbbell
setup_instructions: Stand on one foot on edge of step with dumbbell in hand on affected side. Perform single-leg calf raise through full range with 3-1-3 tempo.
execution_cues: Load to RPE 8
Full range on every rep
Control the lowering — 3 full seconds
Maintain tall posture
common_compensations: Trunk lateral lean to compensate for calf fatigue
contraindications_or_cautions: Highest unilateral load demand. Insertional precaution. Requires solid bilateral HSR tolerance.
patient_facing_explanation: Single-leg heavy loading is the most demanding strength exercise for your Achilles. At this level, you are building the capacity needed for running, jumping, and sport.
clinician_notes: Peak unilateral tendon load in HSR phase. Loading here should approach RPE 8-9. Key exercise for Stage 2-3 transition readiness. Bilateral-to-unilateral strength ratio important benchmark.

setup_instructions: Heavy load on leg press. Perform full plantarflexion range (not past neutral at base) with 3-1-3 tempo.
execution_cues: Significant load — approach RPE 8
Full plantarflexion range
Return only to neutral — no dorsiflexion
3 seconds each phase
contraindications_or_cautions: Insertional-safe with range-of-motion limit to neutral. Requires low irritability.
patient_facing_explanation: Heavy leg press loading is the insertional-safe version of heavy slow resistance. The machine lets us load heavily without the ankle going past neutral.
clinician_notes: HSR for insertional presentations. Best heavy loading option when floor-based raises are contraindicated. Range-of-motion limiter critical.

setup_instructions: Heavy load via Smith machine bar. Full range on raised platform with 3-1-3 tempo. Target RPE 8-9 on final set.
execution_cues: Load heavier than ex_014 — target RPE 8-9
Full range non-negotiable
Slow tempo throughout
No bounce at bottom
common_compensations: Bouncing at bottom under heavy load
contraindications_or_cautions: Insertional precaution. Maximum load potential variant — requires solid progression through earlier HSR exercises.
patient_facing_explanation: The heaviest gym-based version of the calf raise. This level of loading is what drives the strongest structural changes in the tendon.
clinician_notes: Peak bilateral tendon loading. 4x6-8 at RPE 8-9 is the target. Strength gains here support Stage 3 transition. Bilateral-to-unilateral transfer important.

setup_instructions: Standard bilateral calf raise position. Perform quick consecutive rises onto toes with intent for speed and springiness rather than range.
execution_cues: Think speed — fast up and down
Stay on toes between reps
Small, quick movements
Focus on ankle stiffness and spring
common_compensations: Slow, heavy movements rather than fast
Leaving ground with each rep — keep feet on floor initially
contraindications_or_cautions: Bridge exercise between slow HSR and plyometric loading. Do not progress here until 4x6-8 HSR is well tolerated.
patient_facing_explanation: Fast calf raises train your Achilles to store and release energy quickly — a completely different demand from slow exercises. This is the bridge toward jumping and running.
clinician_notes: Rate-of-loading transition. Introduces SSC stimulus at low energy levels. Speed of execution is the variable being trained, not load. Critical bridge to plyometric loading.

setup_instructions: Standing bilateral. Quickly snap onto toes with maximum speed intent. Feet remain on floor. Focus on rate of force development.
execution_cues: Maximum speed on every rep
Snap up — controlled return
Short, sharp movement
Aim for fastest possible ankle action
common_compensations: Performing as a slow calf raise with hurried tempo
contraindications_or_cautions: Requires solid fast calf raise base. More ballistic than ex_024.
patient_facing_explanation: The snap raise trains the explosive power in your calf. This is the kind of speed your tendon needs for running, court sports, and quick directional changes.
clinician_notes: Rate of force development emphasis. Transition toward plyometric stimulus. Monitor for delayed onset tendon symptoms — this is a significant load-rate increase.

setup_instructions: Continuous bilateral fast heel raises for 30-second bouts. Stay on toes, minimal ground contact between reps.
execution_cues: Keep rhythm fast and consistent
Stay on forefoot throughout
Maintain posture
Do not slow down
contraindications_or_cautions: Volume-based fast loading. Monitor total contacts per session.
patient_facing_explanation: Continuous fast heel raises condition your Achilles for the repetitive loading of running — the same rhythm, the same demand, but with both feet on the ground.
clinician_notes: Endurance-fast hybrid. Builds tendon tolerance to repetitive elastic loading. Good running-preparation bridge. Volume monitoring important — count contacts.

setup_instructions: Alternate quick springy steps in place — right, left, right, left. Stay on forefoot throughout. Focus on elastic spring.
execution_cues: Think marching on springs
Minimal foot contact time
Drive upward quickly on each step
Maintain upright posture
contraindications_or_cautions: Introduces alternating single-leg loading at low impact — step toward unilateral plyometrics.
patient_facing_explanation: Alternating rebounds mimic the rhythm of running without leaving the ground. They train your Achilles for the alternating demands of each stride.
clinician_notes: Unilateral loading stimulus within a bilateral framework. Key stepping stone before true plyometric loading and running reintroduction.

setup_instructions: Small bilateral jumps in place with stiff ankle — no knee bend. Focus on minimal ground contact time and elastic spring from ankle only.
execution_cues: Stay stiff — no knee bend
Off the ground and back quickly
Land on forefoot — not flat foot
Short and springy — not high
contraindications_or_cautions: First true plyometric exercise — requires established fast dynamic capacity. Bilateral before unilateral. Monitor next-morning pain carefully.
patient_facing_explanation: Pogos are the foundation of plyometric loading — short, stiff, springy jumps that train your Achilles to store and release energy rapidly. This is the energy-storage function your tendon needs for sport.
clinician_notes: Entry-level plyometric. Contact time target <0.25s. Ankle stiffness is the adaptation driver. Monitor next-morning symptoms. Progress to 100+ contacts/session before advancing.

setup_instructions: Single-leg small hops in place with stiff ankle. Maintain upright posture. Short, springy contacts on forefoot.
execution_cues: Stay stiff — ankle-only spring
Minimal contact time
Stay low — height is not the goal
Consistent rhythm
contraindications_or_cautions: High impact level — requires bilateral pogo tolerance. Formal RSI assessment recommended before progressing to unilateral.
patient_facing_explanation: Single-leg pogos are the most demanding tendon exercise in the programme. They simulate the peak loads of running and jumping on your Achilles — the final step before return to sport.
clinician_notes: RSI target >1.5 (jump height ÷ contact time) for sport readiness. Do not infer readiness from bilateral performance — assess separately. Monitor carefully.

setup_instructions: Stand beside a line. Quick bilateral hops side-to-side over the line. Fast, low hops.
execution_cues: Side-to-side rhythm
Stay on forefoot
Minimal ground contact
Land and go immediately
contraindications_or_cautions: Adds lateral loading demand to bilateral plyometric base. Sport-specific for court and field athletes.
patient_facing_explanation: Lateral hops add a new direction to your tendon loading — important for sports that involve side-to-side movement. They build a more complete resilience in your Achilles.
clinician_notes: Frontal-plane plyometric loading. Important for return to court and field sports. Progress from sagittal-plane bilateral pogos only.

setup_instructions: Hop forward on single leg and land and hold for 3 seconds. Control the landing before the next hop. Build to continuous hops when stick is well controlled.
execution_cues: Hop and stick — hold landing for 3 seconds
Soft landing — control ankle, knee, hip
Look ahead — not down
Build confidence in the landing before removing the hold
common_compensations: Trunk forward lean to manage landing force
contraindications_or_cautions: Deceleration loading — important for injury prevention. Progress from bilateral before unilateral.
patient_facing_explanation: Hopping and sticking the landing builds your ability to control force — not just produce it. This is critical for safe running and cutting movements.
clinician_notes: Deceleration emphasis. Important for ACL and tendon injury prevention. Stick landing is a landing mechanics screen — progress to continuous hops only with good control.

setup_instructions: Continuous forward single-leg hops. Minimal contact time. Build to 200-250 contacts per session across all plyometric exercises.
execution_cues: Maintain consistent rhythm
Minimal ground contact
Stay on forefoot
Aim for 200+ contacts per session total
common_compensations: Slowing significantly by the end of sets
Increased contact time as fatigue accumulates
contraindications_or_cautions: Running readiness threshold: consistent 200+ contacts pain-free + VISA-A ≥80. Requires clinician clearance for return to running.
patient_facing_explanation: Repeated single-leg hops are the final loading step before return to running. When you can complete these consistently without pain, your Achilles is ready for the demands of running.
clinician_notes: Running readiness gate: 200-250 contacts pain-free, next-morning pain ≤2/10, VISA-A ≥80. RSI via drop jump or repeated hop test before clearing for running.

dosage_defaults.reps_or_hold_time: 20 min total (1 min jog : 2 min walk)

setup_instructions: Begin with 1 minute of easy jogging alternating with 2 minutes of walking. Total 20 minutes. Conversational pace only.
execution_cues: Stay at conversational pace — you should be able to talk
Focus on smooth forefoot landing
If pain rises above 3/10, walk only for remainder
Note pain score before and 24h after
common_compensations: Increasing distance before settling on pace
contraindications_or_cautions: Pain threshold during running: ≤3/10. Next-morning pain: ≤2/10 above baseline. Return to running requires CLINICIAN clearance.
patient_facing_explanation: Walk-jog intervals reintroduce running gradually, keeping load manageable while your tendon adapts. Start easy and build confidence — the tendon needs time to adapt to the repetitive loading of running.
clinician_notes: Running reintroduction gate: VISA-A ≥80, 200+ hop contacts pain-free, next-morning pain ≤2/10. Progression: 1:2 → 1:1 → 2:1 jog:walk ratio over weeks. Increase frequency before duration.

setup_instructions: Continuous easy-pace running for 10-20 minutes. Flat surface preferred. RPE 4-5 (easy conversation).
execution_cues: Easy pace — RPE 4-5
Smooth forefoot strike
Increase distance by maximum 10% per week
Stop if pain exceeds 3/10
contraindications_or_cautions: 10% rule: do not increase weekly distance by more than 10%. At least 48h between runs.
patient_facing_explanation: Continuous easy running is the next step — building your running base progressively. Patience here protects your tendon. Small consistent steps are better than rushing.
clinician_notes: Increase distance before pace. Monitor ACWR — do not exceed 1.5 ratio. VISA-A tracking every 2 weeks during running reintroduction phase.

setup_instructions: Run 60m strides at 75-80% effort. Build from easy pace to stride pace over first 20m, hold, decelerate over final 20m.
execution_cues: Build gradually — do not sprint from start
Feel the elastic spring in the ankle
Controlled deceleration
80% feels fast but controlled
contraindications_or_cautions: High rate of loading. Requires established easy running base (20+ minutes continuous). Sport-return preparation.
patient_facing_explanation: Strides introduce faster running speeds progressively. They train your Achilles for the higher forces of sport-pace running without the full volume of a speed session.
clinician_notes: Rate-of-loading increase in running. Introduce only after 3-4 weeks of symptom-stable easy running. Monitor next-morning response closely.

setup_instructions: Walk then jog on gentle hill gradients (5-10%). Begin with uphill walking, progress to uphill jogging. Control downhill carefully.
execution_cues: Uphill before downhill
Short stride on uphill — drive through ankle
Walk downhill initially
Monitor Achilles during downhill — greatest stretch-load
common_compensations: Ignoring increased tendon load on descent
contraindications_or_cautions: High dorsiflexion demand on downhill — insertional contraindicated. Significant tendon loading increase vs flat running.
patient_facing_explanation: Hill running significantly increases the load through your Achilles — especially on the descent. This is important preparation for sport but requires care and gradual introduction.
clinician_notes: Significant tendon load increase vs flat — estimate 20-40% increased Achilles force on incline. Insertional contraindicated throughout. Introduce after flat running is symptom-stable.

required_equipment: seated calf raise machine or weight on knees
setup_instructions: Seated with heavy load on thighs. Perform slow, full-range plantarflexion. Knees at 90° to bias soleus.
execution_cues: Slow controlled movement
Full range
Heavy enough to feel the soleus
Even through both feet
common_compensations: Insufficient load — soleus needs heavy loading to be challenged effectively
contraindications_or_cautions: Soleus is often undertrained relative to gastrocnemius. Insertional-safe throughout.
patient_facing_explanation: Your soleus is one of the most important muscles for Achilles health and is often underworked. This seated exercise targets it directly and is safe for all types of Achilles pain.
clinician_notes: Accessory soleus strengthening — complements main programme. Often undertrained. High load potential is a key feature — do not underdose this exercise.

setup_instructions: Seated or standing. Resistance band around midfoot. Invert foot (turn sole inward) against resistance. Can also be performed with slow walking on inner edge of feet.
execution_cues: Move from the arch — not the toes
Control the return
Feel the inner shin and arch working
Do not compensate with hip rotation
contraindications_or_cautions: Accessory exercise. Supports medial arch control and Achilles load distribution.
patient_facing_explanation: The tibialis posterior supports your arch and influences how load is distributed through your Achilles. Strengthening it reduces strain on the tendon during walking and running.
clinician_notes: Often implicated in overpronation and medial Achilles load increase. Useful adjunct especially where foot posture contributes to tendon loading patterns.

setup_instructions: Side-lying or standing. Band around ankles for resistance. Lift or step affected leg outward against resistance.
execution_cues: Lead with the heel, not the toe
Control the return — do not let it snap back
Maintain pelvic stability
Feel the outside of your hip working
contraindications_or_cautions: Accessory exercise. Hip abductor weakness increases Achilles load through altered gait mechanics.
patient_facing_explanation: Your hip strength directly affects how much load goes through your Achilles during walking and running. Strong hip muscles reduce strain on the tendon and protect it during activity.
clinician_notes: Proximal loading — reduces Achilles strain through improved gait mechanics. Important early adjunct especially in high-irritability phase when direct tendon loading is limited.

target_tissue: Ankle stabilisers, intrinsic foot muscles, gluteus medius
setup_instructions: Single-leg balance on flat or unstable surface. Progress: eyes open flat → eyes closed flat → eyes open foam → add small reaches. Hold each position for 30 seconds.
execution_cues: Soft knee — never locked
Feel the foot working to control balance
Look ahead — not down
Small controlled corrections
common_compensations: Heavy gripping of floor with toes
contraindications_or_cautions: Accessory but important. Proprioceptive deficits are common post-injury and increase re-injury risk.
patient_facing_explanation: Balance training restores the automatic control your ankle and leg need to protect your Achilles during every step. After an Achilles injury, this control is often reduced and needs to be rebuilt.
clinician_notes: Proprioception and neuromuscular control adjunct. Important for reducing re-injury risk, especially on uneven surfaces and return to sport contexts.

exercise_name: Standing Gastrocnemius Wall Stretch (Bilateral, Straight Knee)
setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall approximately 60–80 cm away. Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height for support. Step both feet back to a staggered stance with both heels flat on the floor and knees fully extended (straight). Lean the body gently forward into the wall until a stretch is felt in the calf of the rear leg.
execution_cues: Keep both heels flat on the floor throughout the hold
Maintain a fully straight (extended) knee on the stretching leg
Lean hips gently forward to deepen the stretch — do not bounce
Keep toes pointed straight ahead — avoid toe flare
Breathe normally throughout the hold
Feel the stretch in the belly of the calf, not in the heel
common_compensations: Heel lifting off the floor — reduces stretch on gastrocnemius
Knee bending — shifts stretch from gastrocnemius to soleus
Foot rotating outward (toe flare) — reduces stretch effectiveness
Leaning trunk rather than shifting hip forward
contraindications_or_cautions: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. Do not perform if this exercise provokes pain at the heel insertion site. Prescribe ex_043 or ex_045 instead for insertional presentations.
patient_facing_explanation: This stretch targets the larger of your two calf muscles — the gastrocnemius — which attaches above your knee and runs all the way to your Achilles tendon. A tight gastrocnemius increases the strain on your Achilles during walking and running, so improving its flexibility can reduce tendon stress over time. You must keep your knee straight to stretch this muscle correctly.
clinician_notes: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. Indicated for midportion presentations with WBLT <10 cm or identified gastrocnemius restriction on Silfverskiold test. Bilateral version is the entry-level gastrocnemius stretch. Progress to ex_042 (unilateral) when WBLT approaches 10 cm. Confirm gastrocnemius is the restricted structure before prescribing (compare WBLT knee straight vs. knee bent).

exercise_name: Single-Leg Gastrocnemius Wall Stretch (Unilateral, Straight Knee)
setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall approximately 60–80 cm away. Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height. Step the affected (stretching) leg back so the heel is flat on the floor and the knee is fully extended. The front (non-stretching) leg is slightly bent for balance. Keep the rear heel flat on the floor and lean forward until a firm calf stretch is felt.
execution_cues: Keep the rear heel firmly flat on the floor — this is the critical cue
Keep the rear knee fully straight throughout the hold
Drive the hip of the rear leg forward to deepen the stretch
Keep the rear foot pointed straight ahead
Do not allow the rear foot to rotate outward
Breathe normally throughout the hold
common_compensations: Rear heel lifting — immediately reduces stretch on gastrocnemius
Rear knee bending — switches stretch target from gastrocnemius to soleus
Rear foot toe flare — reduces stretch intensity
Trunk lean rather than hip drive — reduces effectiveness
contraindications_or_cautions: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. Unilateral stretch applies more isolated load through the affected limb — reduce to bilateral (ex_041) if this exercise provokes symptoms >3/10.
patient_facing_explanation: This is the single-leg version of the gastrocnemius stretch, which means all of the stretch is directed through your affected leg. It is more targeted than the bilateral version and is particularly useful when one leg is measurably tighter than the other. Keep your knee completely straight and your heel firmly on the floor to stretch the right muscle.
clinician_notes: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. Progress from ex_041 when bilateral WBLT is approaching 10 cm but side-to-side asymmetry ≥2 cm persists. Unilateral stretch allows targeted management of asymmetric restriction. Monitor for symptom provocation in first session. Progress to ex_046 (WBLT self-mobilization) when WBLT ≥10 cm to address any residual joint mobility contribution.

setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall approximately 40–50 cm away. Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height. Step one foot back (both feet can remain close together for bilateral version). Bend both knees to approximately 30–40 degrees. Keep both heels flat on the floor. Gently drive the knees forward toward the wall, maintaining the bent-knee position, until a deep stretch is felt lower in the calf (below the gastrocnemius belly).
execution_cues: Keep both heels flat on the floor throughout the hold
Maintain a consistent knee bend of approximately 30–40 degrees — do not straighten knees
Drive the knees forward (not just body lean) to deepen the stretch
The stretch should be felt lower and deeper in the calf than a straight-knee stretch
Keep feet hip-width apart and toes pointing forward
Breathe normally throughout
common_compensations: Knees straightening during the hold — shifts stretch to gastrocnemius and reduces soleus isolation
Heels lifting off the floor — reduces stretch on soleus
Excessive forward trunk lean — reduces control and effectiveness
Knees caving inward (valgus) — add ankle/knee alignment cue
contraindications_or_cautions: Safe for insertional presentations — bent-knee position reduces calcaneal compression by reducing passive dorsiflexion demand and slackening the gastrocnemius contribution. If stretch provokes insertional pain, reduce knee bend depth or switch to ex_045 (seated).
patient_facing_explanation: This stretch targets the deeper of your two calf muscles — the soleus — which sits underneath the gastrocnemius and connects directly to your Achilles tendon near the heel. Because the soleus crosses only the ankle (not the knee), bending the knee removes the gastrocnemius from the equation and lets you stretch the soleus in isolation. This stretch is safe even when your Achilles is most sensitive.
clinician_notes: Safe for insertional presentations — bent-knee position reduces calcaneal compression. Preferred first-line stretch for insertional Achilles tendinopathy when stretching is indicated. Also appropriate for high irritability midportion presentations before progressing to straight-knee variants. Use Silfverskiold test to confirm soleus contribution — if dorsiflexion remains restricted with knee flexed, soleus is implicated. Progress to ex_044 (unilateral) when bilateral WBLT (knee flexed) approaches 10 cm with asymmetry ≥2 cm.

setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall with both hands on the wall for support. Place the affected foot approximately 20–30 cm from the wall. Bend the affected knee to approximately 30–40 degrees, keeping the heel flat on the floor. Shift the bent knee forward toward the wall until a deep stretch is felt in the lower calf. The front leg is in the stretching position; the back leg provides light balance support.
execution_cues: Keep the heel of the stretching leg firmly on the floor
Maintain the knee bent to 30–40 degrees throughout — do not allow the knee to straighten
Drive the knee forward over the toe to deepen the stretch
Keep the foot pointed straight ahead — avoid toe flare
The stretch is felt deep and low in the calf, close to the heel
Breathe normally throughout the hold
common_compensations: Knee straightening — reduces soleus isolation and shifts tension to gastrocnemius
Heel lifting — immediately reduces effectiveness of soleus stretch
Foot rotating outward — reduces stretch quality
Insufficient forward knee drive — inadequate stretch depth
contraindications_or_cautions: Safe for insertional presentations — bent-knee position reduces calcaneal compression. Reduce to bilateral (ex_043) if unilateral loading provokes symptoms >3/10. Reduce to seated (ex_045) if standing position is not tolerated.
patient_facing_explanation: This is the single-leg version of the bent-knee soleus stretch, targeting the deep soleus muscle on your affected side specifically. The bent knee keeps the stretch focused on the soleus rather than the gastrocnemius. It is appropriate when one side is measurably tighter than the other or when you have progressed beyond the bilateral version.
clinician_notes: Safe for insertional presentations — bent-knee position reduces calcaneal compression. Progress from ex_043 when bilateral soleus stretch is comfortable and WBLT asymmetry ≥2 cm persists between sides. Unilateral stretch intensifies the load through the affected limb. This is an important exercise for insertional presentations where gastrocnemius stretching is contraindicated but soleus restriction persists. Monitor closely on first session.

exercise_name: Seated Calf Stretch with Towel or Strap
setup_instructions: Sit on the floor or the edge of a firm surface with the affected leg extended in front of you. Loop a towel or resistance band around the ball of the foot. Hold both ends of the towel with hands. Gently pull the towel to draw the foot into dorsiflexion (toes toward you) until a comfortable stretch is felt in the calf. Control the stretch with hand tension.
execution_cues: Keep the knee extended (straight) for gastrocnemius bias, or slightly bent for soleus bias
Pull the towel gently and steadily — do not yank or bounce
Hold the end-point of comfortable stretch for the prescribed duration
Relax the foot actively into the towel rather than just pulling passively
Keep the lower back straight — do not slump
Breathe normally throughout the hold
common_compensations: Pulling into pain rather than comfortable stretch
Knee bending when trying to stretch gastrocnemius — reduces effectiveness
Trunk rounding — reduces stretch quality and may cause back discomfort
Asymmetric pull (one hand harder) — creates ankle inversion during stretch
contraindications_or_cautions: Safe for insertional presentations — non-weight-bearing, clinician-controlled ROM prevents excessive dorsiflexion force. Patient controls the end-range actively via towel tension. Preferred initial stretching option for high irritability presentations or when standing stretches are not tolerated. If foot dorsiflexion provokes insertional pain even with minimal tension, cease and reassess.
patient_facing_explanation: This gentle non-weight-bearing calf stretch uses a towel or band to bring your foot into the stretched position while you are sitting down. Because you are not standing, there is no body weight loading through your ankle, and you have full control over how far the stretch goes. This makes it the safest stretching option and the one most suitable when your tendon is most sensitive.
clinician_notes: Safe for insertional presentations — non-weight-bearing, controlled ROM prevents excessive dorsiflexion force. The gold-standard regression for all standing calf stretches. Use as the primary stretching option in high irritability presentations or where standing stretches provoke symptoms. Progresses to ex_043 (bilateral bent-knee) when tolerated, or ex_041 (bilateral straight-knee) for midportion with low irritability. Also useful for morning stretching in bed before first steps.

target_tissue: gastrocnemius, ankle joint capsule, Achilles tendon
setup_instructions: Stand facing a wall. Place the affected foot directly in front of the wall, with the great toe approximately 8–10 cm from the wall. Keep the heel flat on the floor. Lunge the knee forward to touch the wall while keeping the heel down. If the knee reaches the wall, move the foot back 1–2 cm and repeat until the furthest position is found where heel contact can just be maintained. This simultaneously stretches the calf and mobilises the ankle joint — mirror the WBLT assessment. Hold at end-range for the prescribed duration or perform slow reciprocal touches.
execution_cues: Keep the heel firmly on the floor — do not allow it to lift
Drive the knee directly over the second toe — avoid knee valgus collapse
Find the position where the heel just barely stays down — this is your working range
Hold the end position or perform slow controlled knee drives to the wall
Keep the trunk upright throughout
Measure the toe-to-wall distance — use it to track weekly progress
common_compensations: Heel lifting as the foot moves back — invalidates the stretch and measure
Knee caving inward (valgus) — add 'knee over second toe' cue
Moving the foot too far from the wall — reduces training stimulus
Bouncing the knee — use sustained holds or slow controlled repetitions
contraindications_or_cautions: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. This exercise targets progressive end-range dorsiflexion and is specifically contraindicated where insertional compression is the mechanism of pathology. Use ex_043 or ex_044 instead for insertional presentations.
patient_facing_explanation: This exercise is the active version of the knee-to-wall test your clinician used to assess your ankle flexibility. By slowly working your foot further from the wall over time, you are gently improving the mobility of both your calf muscles and your ankle joint itself. It doubles as both a stretching exercise and a way to track your own progress at home. Record the toe-to-wall distance each week.
clinician_notes: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. This exercise addresses both gastrocnemius extensibility and talocrural joint mobility simultaneously — making it more comprehensive than isolated muscle stretching. Particularly useful when WBLT fails to improve with isolated muscle stretching (suggesting a joint mobility rather than musculotendinous restriction component). Can be performed as measured self-assessment: patient records toe-to-wall distance weekly for home monitoring. Progress to ex_047 (incline board) when WBLT ≥12–14 cm and patient targets further ROM gain for sport return.

setup_instructions: Place the incline board (or wedge) on a flat floor at a 15–30 degree incline angle. Stand with one or both feet on the board with the heel at the lower end and the toes elevated. Keep the knees fully extended (straight). Stand upright and allow body weight to provide a sustained dorsiflexion stretch through the calf and Achilles tendon. Use a wall or support for balance as required. Ensure the incline is at a degree that provides a meaningful but not painful stretch.
execution_cues: Keep the knees fully straight — do not bend the knees
Stand upright — resist the urge to lean forward
Distribute weight evenly across the foot
Allow body weight to provide the stretch — do not force additional range
Breathe normally throughout the hold
Start at a lower incline angle and progress as tolerance improves
common_compensations: Knees bending — significantly reduces gastrocnemius stretch
Leaning forward — reduces effectiveness and alters stretch target
Using too steep an incline on first attempt — provokes pain
Weight shifting to the forefoot only — reduces stretch depth
contraindications_or_cautions: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. The incline board maintains sustained high-range dorsiflexion — this is the highest-demand dorsiflexion exercise in the programme. Prescribe only in low irritability midportion presentations with established WBLT improvement. Do not prescribe if patient has not yet tolerated ex_041 or ex_046 without symptoms.
patient_facing_explanation: The incline board stretch places your foot in a sustained dorsiflexed position using a wedge, allowing your body weight to provide a deep, prolonged stretch to the gastrocnemius muscle and Achilles tendon. This is the most intensive of the stretching exercises in the programme and is appropriate only once your tendon has settled and your ankle flexibility is improving. Start with a shallower angle and build up gradually.
clinician_notes: CONTRAINDICATED for insertional Achilles presentations. Full dorsiflexion range compresses the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. This is the highest dorsiflexion demand stretch in the flexibility programme — prescribe as a final progression for midportion presentations targeting sports return or where significant gastrocnemius restriction persists despite wall stretching. Progress from ex_046 when WBLT ≥12 cm and sport-specific demands require further flexibility. Can be combined with eccentric loading (heel drop on incline board) but this represents a separate loading exercise. Typically prescribed at low irritability stage only.
